title: The Cold Window
subtitle: What really happens between a donor's last heartbeat and a patient's new beginning

scenes.title: Nine thousand kidneys

v.cap: deceased-donor kidneys recovered in 2024 and never transplanted

scenes.say: In 2024, surgeons across this country recovered more than nine thousand kidneys from deceased donors that were never transplanted into anyone. Each one came from a family that said yes on the worst day of their lives. Each one was flown or driven somewhere, logged, tested, and offered. Then it was set aside. Meanwhile, tens of thousands of people sat on a waiting list for exactly that organ. I'm going to spend the next hour walking you through how that happens. Not the brochure version. The real one: the hospital rooms, the phone calls, the machines, the rules, and the people deciding what counts as a usable organ while you wait for a call.

scenes.title: Almost three in ten

v.cap: Of every 100 deceased-donor kidneys recovered in 2024

scenes.say: Here is the same number as a share. According to the national registry's 2024 annual report, twenty-nine point three percent of deceased-donor kidneys recovered for transplant were not transplanted. Look at the grid. Almost three out of every ten. That rate has been climbing for years, even as the number of donors has hit record after record. So this isn't simply a shortage of generous people. It's a problem with what happens after the gift is made. The system calls this nonuse. I'd call it the most expensive silence in American medicine, and by the end of this session, you'll understand where the silence comes from and what you can do to break it.

scenes.title: Watch it your way
scenes.say: We'll follow a donated organ the way it actually travels: from the moment someone becomes a potential donor, through recovery, preservation, the offer system, transport, and finally surgery. At each stop, I'll show you who's in charge, what can go wrong, and the newest science trying to fix it. You can pause me any time, jump between chapters, or slow me down. Along the way, Navigator Tips will appear beside me with specific questions to ask and rules to cite. Every chapter ends with a short question. These aren't tests. They're checkpoints, because some of what you're about to learn changes how you should talk to your own care team.

scenes.title: Brain death and circulatory death

items: Heart still beating on a ventilator
Death declared after the heart stops
Organs face a stretch of warm ischemia

scenes.say: Every deceased donation begins with one of two legal definitions of death. In donation after brain death, a person's brain has permanently stopped functioning, but a ventilator keeps the heart beating, so the organs keep receiving blood right up until recovery. In donation after circulatory death, the person has a devastating injury but doesn't meet brain death criteria. The family decides to withdraw life support, the heart stops, a waiting period passes, death is declared, and only then can the surgical team begin. In those minutes between the last heartbeat and the start of cooling, the organs are warm and starved of oxygen. Surgeons call it warm ischemia, and it's the reason these organs have historically been treated as riskier.

scenes.title: The minutes nobody describes
scenes.say: Let me slow that second pathway down, because families are rarely walked through it. After a family decides to withdraw life support, the clock starts. Each hospital and procurement organization works under a protocol with a time limit. If the heart doesn't stop within that window, often an hour or two, donation is called off and the person is cared for until they die naturally. If the heart does stop, there's a hands-off period of a few minutes, when no one touches the patient, to confirm circulation won't return on its own. Only then is death declared. Every one of those minutes is a moment where trust is either earned or lost.

scenes.title: From 2 percent to half of all donors

v.lab: Circulatory-death donors as a share of all deceased donors

scenes.src: Husain et al., JAMA 2026; HRSA OPTN briefing paper
scenes.say: Here's a shift almost nobody outside the field has noticed. In 2000, circulatory-death donors made up about two percent of deceased donors in the United States: one hundred eighteen people. By 2025, a study in the Journal of the American Medical Association counted more than eight thousand, roughly half of all deceased donors. Nearly half of recovered kidneys now come through this pathway. That growth is a big part of why transplant numbers keep setting records. It's also why the questions in the next few chapters matter so much. When half the system runs on a pathway built around a stopped heart, how that moment is handled becomes everything.

scenes.title: Your organ offer may say DCD

items: How long was the warm time?
Would you decline it for every patient, or just me?

scenes.say: If you're waiting for a kidney, you may one day hear that an offer is a DCD kidney, short for donation after circulatory death. You might also hear that it's more likely to start slowly. That's true on average. Kidneys from these donors have higher rates of delayed function, meaning the new kidney takes days or weeks to fully wake up. But delayed function is not failure. Many of these kidneys go on to work well for years. The real questions are how long the warm period lasted, how the organ was preserved, and whether your team is declining it because of you specifically, or because of a habit.

tip.t: Ask your transplant team in writing which kinds of offers they automatically screen out for you, such as DCD donors, older donors, or long cold times. Then ask whether those limits still fit your situation today.

scenes.title: Quick question
scenes.say: Let's make sure that distinction stuck.

q.p: What's the main reason circulatory-death organs have been treated as riskier?
o: The donors are always older
Warm, oxygen-starved minutes after the heart stops
They can only travel short distances
They're never tested for infection
q.why: After the heart stops and before cooling begins, the organ is warm and without oxygen. That warm ischemia is the core injury preservation science is trying to reduce.

scenes.title: Fifty-five monopolies

v.cap: 55 organ procurement organizations, each with an exclusive territory

scenes.src: Federal designation; territories set in the 1980s
scenes.say: When a hospital patient may become a donor, the hospital must call the local organ procurement organization, usually shortened to OPO. There are fifty-five of them. Each one holds an exclusive territory, a map line drawn decades ago, so nobody competes. The OPO evaluates the patient, approaches the family, manages the donor's body, coordinates the surgeons, and offers the organs through the national match system. These are nonprofits, funded through Medicare cost reimbursement, and for most of their history no one was ever pushed out. Until very recently, none had lost its federal certification in roughly forty years. That changed in 2025, and it's still changing as you watch this.

scenes.title: Your doctors are not the donation team

items: Full life-saving care for every patient
Refer potential donors to the OPO
Keep medical care separate from donor status
Give families adequate time to decide
Stop immediately if signs of life appear

scenes.say: In March 2026, Medicare sent new guidance to every state inspection agency spelling out who does what. Hospitals must give every patient the same full, life-saving care regardless of whether they might become a donor, and must keep that care separate from donor status. Procurement organizations and hospitals must give families adequate time to decide, without rushing or pressure. And if signs of life are observed before or during recovery, procurement is expected to stop immediately. Inspectors now review referral records, complaints, and cases where procurement stopped before recovery. None of this was new law. It was a reminder that had to be issued, which tells you how badly it was needed.

tip.h: Ask who each person works for
tip.t: In an ICU, ask every new person who joins a family conversation: are you part of the medical team, or the donation organization? You have the right to know, and to ask for time before any decision.

scenes.title: 351 cases, examined line by line

v.cap: HRSA review of donations authorized but not completed, 2021 to 2024

scenes.src: HHS and HRSA findings on Network for Hope
scenes.say: In Kentucky, a federal agency called HRSA reviewed three hundred fifty-one cases where donation was authorized but never completed at the procurement organization now called Network for Hope. It found one hundred three cases with concerning features, including seventy-three patients showing neurological signs incompatible with organ donation. Federal reviewers concluded that at least twenty-eight patients may not have been dead when the procurement process began. The organization has disputed the findings and says it follows national policy. Investigators also noted that the risks were highest in smaller and rural hospitals, where staff may have less experience and less backup. That's not a footnote. That's where many donors are.

scenes.title: A decertification, and an appeal

ev: Jul 2025
HHS announces reform initiative after the Kentucky findings
Sep 2025
First OPO decertification in decades
HHS begins decertifying Network for Hope
CMS termination date in its public notice

scenes.src: CMS public notice; HHS press release, Aug 5, 2026
scenes.say: In August 2026, the Department of Health and Human Services announced it was decertifying Network for Hope, which serves Kentucky and parts of Indiana, Ohio, and West Virginia. The public notice set November third as the date its Medicare agreement would end. The organization strongly disagrees and has said it will appeal. Whatever the outcome, notice what had to happen first: a whistleblower, a congressional hearing, newspaper investigations, and years of federal review. The system didn't catch this on its own. People outside it forced the issue. Hold onto that, because it's the same lesson you'll see in every chapter of this webinar.

tip.t: Look up which procurement organization covers your county. Families can ask the hospital's ethics committee or patient advocate to be present during donation conversations, and can ask for any step to be explained before agreeing.

scenes.title: Quick question
scenes.say: One question on the gatekeepers.

q.p: How many organ procurement organizations hold exclusive territories in the United States?
o: About 12
Every hospital has its own
q.why: Fifty-five OPOs each hold a federally designated territory. Until recently, almost none faced real consequences for poor performance.

scenes.title: A pump after the heart stops

v.label: NRP: warm blood restored to the abdominal or chest organs inside the donor

scenes.say: Now to one of the most important, least discussed procedures in organ donation. It's called normothermic regional perfusion, or NRP. After a circulatory-death donor's heart stops and death is declared, surgeons connect an external pump that restores warm, oxygen-rich blood to selected organs, while the vessels leading to the brain are blocked. The organs get to recover from those warm, starved minutes before they're removed, and they can be assessed while working. Supporters say it rescues organs that would otherwise be lost and produces better transplants. Some surgeons call it life-saving care that, done properly, is safe. That's one side of a very sharp debate.

scenes.title: The dead donor rule

v.q: It's taking organs from people who are no longer dead.
v.by: Dr. Lainie Friedman Ross, bioethicist, University of Rochester, to NPR

scenes.say: Here's the objection. Organ donation in this country rests on something called the dead donor rule: recovery must never cause death. A circulatory-death declaration means no one will try to restart circulation. NRP restarts circulation. Critics, including bioethicists and some transplant surgeons, argue that this contradicts the very declaration it depends on, and that clamping the brain's blood supply is an attempt to make sure a second kind of death has happened. They also worry that families aren't always told, in plain words, what NRP involves before they agree to donate. Both sides are serious people. You deserve to hear both arguments before anyone asks your family to decide.

scenes.title: Will NRP be used? Ask before you sign.

items: Will NRP be used for our loved one?
Who will be in the room, and who do they work for?
What happens if there are signs of life?
Can we stop the process at any point?
Will we get a written summary afterward?

scenes.src: OPTN NRP policy: authorization and disclosure safeguards
scenes.say: If you ever find yourself in that room, as a family member or a health care proxy, here are questions worth asking out loud. Will NRP be used? Who will be present, and who employs them? What happens if anyone sees signs of life? Can we stop at any point? And will we receive a written summary of what was done? The new national policy includes requirements around authorization and disclosure, but a policy only protects people who know to invoke it. Asking these questions isn't hostile. It's what an informed family does. Most donation professionals will respect you more for it, and the ones who don't are telling you something.

scenes.title: A national policy, approved by emergency

items: Clamp and vent the vessels to the brain
Avoid paralytic drugs that could mask movement
Plan to hand care back if concerns arise
Report unexpected events to the OPTN

scenes.say: On November sixth, 2026, the national transplant network's board approved the first uniform national policy for NRP, through an emergency action so safeguards could start right away. Among other things, surgeons must do more than clamp the vessels to the brain; they must also vent them. The policy recommends against paralyzing drugs that could hide movement. Procurement organizations need a documented plan for handing care back to the hospital team if concerns arise. And certain events, like an unplanned pause over concern that blood may be reaching the brain, must be reported. Critics say these steps mostly describe what careful surgeons already do. Supporters call it an important first step.

tip.t: The NRP policy is open for public comment from November 13 to December 28, 2026, on the OPTN website. Anyone can comment. A specific, personal, well-reasoned comment becomes part of the official record.

scenes.title: Quick question
scenes.say: Let's check the core of this debate.

q.p: Why do critics say NRP conflicts with the dead donor rule?
o: It uses organs from living donors
It restarts circulation after death was declared based on circulation stopping
It's only done in other countries
It skips family consent entirely
q.why: A circulatory-death declaration assumes circulation won't be restarted. NRP restarts it to the organs, which is the heart of the ethical objection.

scenes.title: Cold slows the damage. It doesn't stop it.

v.cap: Cold ischemia: from the cold flush until blood flows again in the recipient

scenes.say: Once an organ is removed, it's flushed with a cold preservation solution and chilled. This begins cold ischemia, the window this foundation is named after. Cold slows the organ's metabolism to a crawl, the way a refrigerator slows spoiling. But the cells are still using up their energy, and toxic byproducts are still building. When blood finally rushes back in the recipient, there's a second wave of injury, called reperfusion injury. So every hour on ice matters. Not because an organ suddenly expires at a certain hour, but because the damage keeps adding up, quietly, in a cooler, in a cargo hold, on a loading dock, while people make phone calls.

scenes.title: KDPI: the number that decides a kidney's fate

v.cap: Share of recovered kidneys not transplanted, 2024

scenes.say: Every deceased-donor kidney gets a score called the Kidney Donor Profile Index, or KDPI. It runs from zero to one hundred percent and compares that kidney with others recovered the previous year, using the donor's age, size, history, and a few lab values. A higher number means a shorter expected lifespan for the kidney, on average. Here's why it matters. In 2024, about forty-one percent of kidneys that were biopsied went unused, and nearly sixty-nine percent of kidneys from donors sixty-five or older did. For many older patients, a kidney from an older donor today can beat years more of waiting for a perfect one. But only if someone accepts it.

scenes.title: Longer cold time, slower starts

v.cap: Delayed graft function by cold ischemia time, U.S. recipients 2000 to 2018

scenes.say: Here's what a large national study of U.S. kidney recipients found. With sixteen hours of cold time or less, about twenty-one percent of kidneys had delayed function. Between thirty-two and forty hours, it was about thirty-seven and a half percent. So longer cold time clearly means more slow starts. But here's what the same researchers concluded, and it surprises people: the effect on long-term kidney survival was modest, and smaller than the effect of the donor's own profile. They warned that long cold time alone should not be the main reason to decline a kidney. That one sentence describes thousands of discarded organs.

scenes.kicker: A different country, a different answer
scenes.title: Would these kidneys be thrown away elsewhere?

v.cap: of discarded U.S. kidneys estimated usable under French allocation practices

scenes.src: Aubert et al., 2019, as summarized in a 2024 review
scenes.say: Here's a comparison that should bother everyone. A 2019 study applied France's kidney practices to American kidneys that had been discarded, and estimated that sixty-two percent of them could have been successfully transplanted there. France isn't using magic. It's using organs from older donors more readily, relying less on rushed biopsies, and treating long-term outcomes rather than perfect paperwork as the goal. Researchers here have also questioned how well a biopsy read in the middle of the night predicts how a kidney will really do. When a different country looks at the same kidney and sees a life-saving organ, the problem isn't the kidney. It's the decision.

scenes.title: Most of the clock is spent waiting

v.cap: average kidney allocation time as of June 2025

scenes.say: Where do those hours go? Surgery takes a few. Flying takes a few. But a huge share is spent on allocation: the process of offering the kidney down a ranked list of patients until a transplant team says yes. As of mid-2025, the national transplant network reported the average kidney allocation time at nearly twenty hours. Twenty hours of offers, declines, callbacks, and waiting for test results, often while the organ sits on ice. Each decline pushes the kidney further down the list and further into the clock, which makes the next team more likely to decline too. It's a spiral, and once it starts, it's very hard to stop.

tip.h: Ask about speed, not just safety
tip.t: Ask your transplant program how quickly it responds to offers, and whether it will accept a kidney that has already been declined by others. Slow responses add hours to the clock for everyone behind you.

scenes.title: Quick question
scenes.say: Here's a question about that cold-time study.

q.p: What did the national cold-time study conclude about declining kidneys?
o: Any kidney over 24 hours should be discarded
Long cold time alone shouldn't be the main reason to decline
Cold time has no effect at all
Only living-donor kidneys are worth accepting
q.why: Longer cold time raised delayed function, but the effect on long-term survival was modest. The authors cautioned against declining a kidney on cold time alone, especially when the donor profile is good.

scenes.title: Static cold storage: the 1970s standard

v.label: Static cold storage: solution, bags, ice, and a cooler

scenes.say: For more than fifty years, the standard way to move a kidney has looked a lot like a picnic. The organ is flushed, sealed in sterile bags with preservation fluid, and packed in ice inside a cooler. It's simple, cheap, and it travels anywhere. It also gives the team almost no information. Nobody can see how the organ is doing inside that cooler. They can only count the hours and guess. That is the backdrop for everything you're about to see: a field trying to move from guessing to measuring, and from slowing damage to actually preventing it.

scenes.title: Hypothermic machine perfusion

v.label: Cold solution pumped through the kidney's own vessels

scenes.say: The first upgrade is a cold pump, called hypothermic machine perfusion. Instead of sitting still in fluid, the kidney is connected to a machine that pushes cold preservation solution through its own blood vessels. That keeps the tiny vessels open, flushes out waste, and gives the team numbers to watch, like flow and resistance. A Cochrane review, one of the most respected forms of medical evidence, concluded that compared with the icebox, cold pumping reduces delayed function, improves kidney survival, and is cost-saving in U.S. and European settings. That's not a lab curiosity. That's established evidence, and many American kidneys still travel on ice.

scenes.title: The COMPARE trial

v.cap: Kidneys that failed within the first year, paired circulatory-death donors aged 50+

scenes.say: Then researchers asked a simple question: what if we add oxygen to the cold pump? In a European trial called COMPARE, published in The Lancet, kidney pairs from older circulatory-death donors were split. One kidney from each donor got a cold pump with oxygen, the other got the same pump without it. Same donor, same day, a near-perfect comparison. In the first year, three of one hundred six oxygenated kidneys failed, compared with eleven of one hundred six without oxygen. The difference in average kidney function wasn't significant, but complications and failures dropped. Oxygen, even at cold temperatures, seems to matter.

scenes.title: Normothermic machine perfusion

v.label: Body-temperature, oxygenated red-cell perfusate: the kidney works outside the body

scenes.say: The boldest approach skips the cold entirely. In normothermic machine perfusion, the kidney is kept at body temperature and fed a warm, oxygenated fluid made with red blood cells. The organ actually works on the machine, making urine, using energy, showing whether it's viable. A randomized trial in circulatory-death kidneys found that one hour of this warm perfusion was safe and feasible, but it didn't reduce delayed function compared with the icebox. Then, in 2025, an Oxford-led study kept kidneys on warm perfusion for a median of about six hours, and as long as twenty-three, before transplant. The results are early but they hint at a future where organs are tested, treated, and even repaired before surgery.

scenes.title: Livers and hearts went first

ev: Sep 2021
FDA approves a warm perfusion system for donor livers
Dec 2021
A second warm liver device approved, up to 12 hours
Apr 2022
Warm heart system approved for circulatory-death donors
Today
Kidneys still travel mostly cold

scenes.src: FDA premarket approvals P200031, P200035; BioWorld
scenes.say: Warm machines aren't science fiction for every organ. In 2021, the FDA approved two warm perfusion systems for donor livers, one of them for up to twelve hours of preservation. In 2022, a warm system was approved for hearts from circulatory-death donors, which means a heart can be restarted and watched beating in a box before it's ever placed in a recipient. For years, those hearts were considered impossible to use. So the question isn't whether warm, measured preservation works. It's why kidneys, the organ the most people are waiting for, still mostly travel in coolers. Part of the answer is cost. Part of it is habit. Neither is a medical reason.

scenes.title: The machine may matter as much as the match

items: Do you use machine perfusion for kidneys?
Do you accept pumped kidneys from far away?

scenes.say: So here's the practical takeaway. When you're choosing a transplant program, or deciding whether to list at more than one, ask how they preserve kidneys and what they're willing to accept. Programs that use machine perfusion, and know how to read its numbers, may say yes to organs that others decline. And if you hear a kidney was declined because of long cold time, it's fair to ask whether it was on a pump, and what the pump showed. You're not second-guessing your surgeon. You're asking the same questions the research is asking.

tip.t: The Scientific Registry of Transplant Recipients publishes program-specific reports at srtr.org, including how often each program accepts the offers it receives. Compare programs before you choose where to list.

scenes.title: Quick question
scenes.say: A question about that trial.

q.p: In the COMPARE trial, what happened when oxygen was added to cold machine perfusion?
o: More kidneys failed
Fewer kidneys failed in the first year
Kidneys could only be used locally
Nothing was measured
q.why: Three of 106 oxygenated kidneys failed versus 11 of 106 without oxygen. Even at cold temperatures, supplying oxygen appears to protect the organ.

scenes.title: What if the clock met oxygen instead of only cold?

v.cap: Biological Hemoglobin Oxygen Carrier: hemoglobin working outside the red cell

scenes.say: Every technology you've just seen points to the same idea: organs suffer because they're starved of oxygen, and cold only slows that harm. Which leads to a question few patients ever hear asked. What if we could deliver oxygen to an organ precisely, without needing whole blood? That's the work of BHOC Therapeutics. BHOC stands for Biological Hemoglobin Oxygen Carrier. It's hemoglobin, the molecule your red cells use to carry oxygen, working outside the red cell. Because there's no cell membrane, it carries no blood-group markers, so it's designed to be compatible with all blood types. And its oxygen affinity is engineered, so it loads oxygen and releases it where tissue needs it.

scenes.title: Why oxygen carriers must earn trust

v.cap: patients in 16 trials of earlier hemoglobin-based blood substitutes reviewed in 2008

scenes.say: You should also know the history, because it explains why careful evidence matters so much here. In 2008, a review in the Journal of the American Medical Association looked at sixteen trials of earlier hemoglobin-based blood substitutes, five products, three thousand seven hundred eleven patients. Those earlier products, given as blood substitutes, were linked to a higher risk of heart attack and death. That's a sobering record, and it's exactly why BHOC Therapeutics' evidence hub keeps historical oxygen-carrier studies separate from wider transplantation research, so neither borrows credibility from the other. Any new approach has to earn trust from scratch, in the right setting, with the right trials. That's the standard we should hold everyone to.

scenes.title: Not a replacement for blood

l.h: What BHOC is designed to be
items: Compatible with all blood types by design

scenes.say: BHOC Therapeutics calls its approach Precision Oxygen Therapeutics: oxygen delivery that's controlled and predictable, down to the tissue. And they're unusually careful about what they don't claim. They don't call it artificial blood. It's not designed to replace blood. It's meant to be a complementary bridge for oxygen delivery. Their research areas include organ transplantation, severe anemia, surgery and blood loss, cardiac and ischemic emergencies, sickle cell disease, and emergency and remote care. And they state plainly that these are areas of research and development, not approved therapeutic claims. In a field full of hype, that honesty is worth noticing.

scenes.title: Mapping oxygen across the graft's journey
scenes.say: For transplantation, BHOC Therapeutics maintains an evidence hub mapping sixty-four publications on oxygen carriers, across liver, kidney, heart, lung, limb, and composite tissue research. It asks one question at four moments. During preservation, while the organ waits. During machine perfusion, when oxygen is delivered outside the body. During viability assessment, when teams judge whether an organ can be used. And at reperfusion, when blood flows again in the recipient. The first of those moments is the cold window itself. Cold storage slows the damage. Controlled oxygen delivery asks whether some of that damage never has to happen at all.

link.label: Explore the BHOC transplant evidence hub

scenes.kicker: Why patients never hear about this
scenes.title: It lives in journals, not in exam rooms
scenes.say: None of this is secret. It's published and presented. But it's discussed almost entirely among surgeons, preservation scientists, and companies. It almost never reaches the person actually waiting for an organ, or the care partner who will manage the first hard weeks after surgery. That gap matters. Better preservation could mean organs travel farther, more of them are judged usable, and fewer people start their new life with a kidney that's slow to wake up. That's directly relevant to whether a specific patient in a specific region gets an offer at all. You deserve to know what's being built to solve the problem that keeps you waiting.

tip.t: When you read about any new preservation technology, ask three things: was it tested in people, was it randomized, and is it approved for use? Listing a study is not the same as proving a treatment works.

scenes.title: Quick question
scenes.say: Let's make sure the description of BHOC is clear.

q.p: Which description of BHOC matches how BHOC Therapeutics describes it?
o: Artificial blood that replaces transfusions
Cell-free hemoglobin designed to be compatible with all blood types
An approved treatment for kidney failure
A new kind of dialysis filter
q.why: BHOC Therapeutics describes BHOC as cell-free hemoglobin with engineered oxygen affinity, designed to be compatible with all blood types, as a complementary oxygen bridge. They state their transplant work is research, not an approved claim.

scenes.title: Declined on your behalf

v.cap: median kidney offers received by patients who died waiting

scenes.src: Research cited by the National Kidney Foundation
scenes.say: Here's something most people on the list never realize. Under federal law, organ offers are made to individual patients, not to transplant centers. But it's the center that answers the phone. Your team can decline an offer made in your name, and in most cases you'll never hear about it. Research cited by the National Kidney Foundation found that patients who died waiting had received a median of twenty-five kidney offers before death. Twenty-five. Some of those organs were surely wrong for them. But it's worth asking whether every single one was. And it's worth asking why the person whose life depended on the answer was never told the question existed.

scenes.title: Caution has incentives

items: Slow starts mean longer hospital stays

scenes.say: Why would a team decline an organ that might help you? Usually not out of carelessness. Programs are graded publicly on how their transplants turn out, so a risky kidney that struggles can hurt their numbers. Kidneys that start slowly mean longer hospital stays and more work. Offers often arrive at night, when staffing is thin. Many researchers have argued that these pressures push centers toward saying no, even when a patient would gladly take the risk. Regulators have started measuring offer acceptance alongside outcomes for exactly this reason. Your job isn't to overrule your surgeon. It's to make sure your own tolerance for risk is on the record.

scenes.title: Out-of-sequence allocation

v.lab: Kidneys allocated out of the national match sequence

scenes.src: OPTN AOOS Workgroup, September 2025; HRSA directive, February 2025
scenes.say: Now the part that has federal regulators most concerned. When procurement organizations worry a kidney won't be placed in time, some have stopped following the ranked list and offered it directly to a center they know will take it. That's called allocation out of sequence. According to the chair of the national workgroup studying it, it rose from about one percent of kidney allocations in 2019 to roughly eighteen percent in 2024. In February 2025, HRSA told the transplant network that widespread out-of-sequence placement, as practiced, doesn't comply with federal rules, and that offers must go to individual patients, not to programs. When the line gets skipped, someone in that line lost a chance and never knew it.

scenes.title: What you can ask for now

items: Your current waitlist status, active or inactive
Your offer filters and acceptance criteria
Whether offers were declined for you, and why

scenes.src: HHS IOTA proposal, Dec 2025; OPTN patient notification proposal, 2025
scenes.say: There is movement. In December 2025, federal health officials proposed changes to a Medicare model for kidney transplant hospitals, including notifying patients who've been listed for three years about offers declined on their behalf. The national network has also considered requiring programs to notify patients within ten business days when they're made inactive or reactivated. These are proposals and pilots, not universal rights yet. But nothing stops you from asking today. Ask in writing for your status, your offer filters, your waiting time, and whether offers have been declined for you. A program that respects you will answer. A program that won't is telling you something important.

tip.t: You can sit on the list as inactive, unable to receive offers, without knowing it. Ask your coordinator every three months, in writing: am I active, and has anything changed in my status or offer criteria?

scenes.title: Listing at a second program
scenes.say: One of the most effective moves patients rarely hear about is listing at more than one transplant program. It's allowed. Programs differ widely in what they accept, how fast they respond, and how many offers they turn down. A second program, especially one in a different procurement region, can mean a completely different stream of offers. It isn't right for everyone. It takes extra testing, travel planning, and insurance approval. Ask the second program how your waiting time would be counted and what they'd need from you. And ask your first program directly how it feels about patients who list elsewhere. Their answer will tell you a lot.

scenes.title: Quick question
scenes.say: A question about who actually receives an offer.

q.p: Under federal rules, to whom is an organ offer actually made?
o: The transplant center
The procurement organization
The individual patient
The patient's insurer
q.why: Offers are made to individual patients. Centers respond on the patient's behalf, which is exactly why patients should ask what's being declined in their name.

ev: Aug 2024
OPTN board incorporated separately from its longtime contractor
Independent, elected board seated; multi-vendor model begins
New out-of-sequence dashboards and compliance tools
Contracts and oversight still being restructured

scenes.say: For nearly forty years, the national transplant network was run under one main contract by one organization. That's changing. HRSA separated the network's board from its longtime contractor, seated an independent elected board, and moved to a model with multiple vendors handling different jobs. It added dashboards for out-of-sequence allocation and new compliance tools, and it opened a direct channel for reporting concerns. Change on this scale is messy, and not everything is working smoothly. But for the first time in a generation, the doors are open to people outside the industry. Patients and care partners can comment, report, and sit on committees.

tip.t: Concerns about organ donation, procurement, or transplant practices can be sent to HRSA through the OPTN complaint channel at OPTNComplaints@hrsa.gov. Include dates, places, and what you observed.

scenes.title: Procurement organizations, graded

v.cap: AOPO warned up to 42% of the 55 OPOs could face decertification

scenes.src: CMS final rule CMS-3409-F, Oct 30, 2026; Bloomberg Government
scenes.say: Meanwhile, Medicare finalized a rule on October thirtieth, 2026, that keeps its three-tier grading system for procurement organizations and moves toward decertifying the lowest tier. Organizations whose service areas fall only in tier three will be decertified, and the best performers can compete to take over. The industry's own association warned that as many as forty-two percent of the fifty-five organizations could face decertification. Current agreements are set to expire in January 2027. Whatever you think of the metrics, this is the first time the gatekeepers have faced real competition. Your region's organ procurement organization may soon be run by someone new.

scenes.title: The bottom tier shrank

v.cap: Lowest-performing OPOs as counted by CMS

scenes.src: CMS proposed rule fact sheet, January 2026
scenes.say: Here's the encouraging part. When Medicare first published its grading system, it estimated that a large share of procurement organizations would fall into the lowest tier. According to Medicare's own 2026 fact sheet, the number of organizations in tier three has since dropped from twenty-four to ten. Some of that is real improvement: better referral systems, more circulatory-death donation, more organs recovered. The lesson is simple and it applies to your own advocacy too. Organizations change when they're measured in public and when consequences are real. Patients and families helped make that pressure possible, by testifying, writing, and refusing to let the subject drop.

scenes.title: Quick question
scenes.say: One more on accountability.

q.p: What happens to a procurement organization whose service areas are all graded tier 3 under the 2026 rule?
o: It gets extra funding
Nothing changes
It will be decertified
It merges with a hospital
q.why: Under the final rule, OPOs with only tier 3 service areas will be decertified, and higher-performing organizations can compete for those territories.

scenes.title: Gene-edited pig kidneys enter trials

ev: First pig kidney transplant into a living person
Jan 2025
Tim Andrews receives a gene-edited pig kidney
FDA clears the first formal clinical trials
Jan 2026
Andrews receives a human kidney after nearly nine months off treatment

scenes.say: Let me take you to the edge of what's possible. Gene-edited pig kidneys have moved from experiments into formal clinical trials. One company is testing a kidney with ten gene edits; another is testing one with sixty-nine. In January 2025, a New Hampshire man named Tim Andrews received a pig kidney at Massachusetts General Hospital and lived nearly nine months without needing dialysis. Then, in January 2026, he received a human kidney. The pig kidney served as a bridge. Researchers are careful to say much more testing is needed. But the idea that a person's wait could someday be measured in weeks, not years, is no longer science fiction.

scenes.title: Organ banking

v.cap: vitrified rat kidneys stored, rewarmed, and transplanted with full function

scenes.src: Han et al., Nature Communications, 2023 (University of Minnesota)
scenes.say: Now imagine never racing the clock at all. In 2023, researchers at the University of Minnesota cooled rat kidneys so fast, in a protective solution, that they turned glassy instead of forming ice. They stored them for up to one hundred days, then rewarmed them evenly from the inside using tiny iron particles and a magnetic field. The kidneys were transplanted, and all five recipient rats regained full kidney function within a month. These were rats, not people, and human organs are far bigger and harder to rewarm. But if organ banking ever works in humans, transplant could become a planned surgery instead of a midnight emergency.

scenes.title: Every breakthrough runs into the same wall

items: Patients left out of the loop

scenes.say: Step back and you'll see the pattern. The science is moving fast: warm machines, oxygen carriers, gene-edited organs. But every one of those advances has to pass through the same system. A procurement organization has to refer the donor properly. A center has to answer an offer quickly. A team has to be willing to accept an organ that's been pumped and measured instead of guessed at. A patient has to know they're active and what's being declined. Technology can add hours to the clock. Only people can make sure those hours aren't wasted. That's where you come in, and that's where this foundation lives.

scenes.title: Quick question
scenes.say: A question about the far horizon.

q.p: What did the University of Minnesota organ banking study achieve?
o: Human kidneys stored for a year
Rat kidneys stored up to 100 days, then transplanted with full function
A kidney grown from stem cells
A permanent artificial kidney
q.why: Vitrified rat kidneys were stored up to 100 days, rewarmed with nanoparticles, and transplanted. All five recipients recovered full function within 30 days. Human use is still far off.

scenes.title: Five moves for patients and care partners

items: Confirm in writing that you're active
Ask for your offer filters and acceptance criteria
Ask how your program preserves kidneys
Compare programs' offer acceptance at srtr.org
Consider listing at a second program

scenes.say: Let's turn all of this into action. If you or someone you love is waiting, here are five moves for this week. Confirm in writing that you're active. Ask for your offer filters, meaning the kinds of organs your team automatically turns down for you, and whether they still make sense. Ask how your program preserves kidneys and whether it uses machine perfusion. Look up your program's offer acceptance data on the national registry's website. And ask whether listing at a second program could shorten your wait. None of these requires a medical degree. Each one puts you back in the room where decisions about your life are being made.

scenes.title: Your rights in the hardest room

items: Full medical care comes first, always
You can ask for time, and you'll get it
You can ask who each person works for
You can ask whether NRP will be used
You can ask for the hospital's patient advocate

scenes.say: If you're ever the family in that hospital room, here's what you can hold onto. Your loved one must receive full medical care, whatever the donation question. You can ask for time, and federal guidance says you should get it, without pressure. You can ask every person who joins the conversation who they work for. You can ask whether normothermic regional perfusion will be used. And you can ask for the hospital's patient advocate or ethics consult to be with you. Saying yes to donation is one of the most generous things a person can do. It should never be a yes given in confusion.

scenes.title: If you see something, document it

items: Write down what you saw, with times
Use your hospital's safety reporting system
Contact your state survey agency if needed

scenes.say: Some of you watching work inside hospitals. If you ever see something during a donation case that troubles you, write it down right away: what you saw, when, and who was present. Use your hospital's safety reporting system. You can also report directly to HRSA through the transplant network's complaint channel, and to your state's survey agency, which inspects hospitals for Medicare. The Kentucky case came to light because people inside the system refused to stay quiet. Their courage changed national policy. Speaking up isn't disloyalty to your profession. It's the highest form of loyalty to it.

scenes.title: Turn knowledge into a public record

items: Comment on the NRP policy before Dec 28, 2026
Write to your members of Congress about offer transparency
Ask your county's OPO for its CMS tier and plans
Share one fact from this webinar with sources

scenes.say: Next, the public record. Institutions respond to written, specific, sourced comments, not to frustration in a waiting room. Before December twenty-eighth, 2026, submit a comment on the national NRP policy, whatever your view. Write to your members of Congress asking them to support offer transparency for every patient, not just a pilot. Ask your region's procurement organization what tier it's in and what it's doing about it. And share one fact you learned today, with the source attached. One sourced fact, posted by a real person, does more than a thousand angry comments without one.

tip.t: In any comment or letter, include one personal fact, one data point with its source, and one specific request. Keep it under a page. Staff summarize what they can quote.

scenes.title: Last question
scenes.say: Here's the last checkpoint.

q.p: Under CMS's 2026 guidance, what should happen if signs of life are seen during procurement?
o: Continue if the family agreed
Pause for an hour, then continue
Stop the procurement process immediately
Ask the transplant center to decide
q.why: CMS guidance says OPOs are expected to stop the procurement process immediately if signs of life are observed before or during organ recovery.

scenes.title: Bring this to your community

v.cap: Movements start with a few people who refuse to look away

scenes.say: Finally, don't carry this alone. The Cold Ischemia Foundation exists to put this knowledge in the hands of the people the system was supposed to serve, with no industry money behind us. Join us as a volunteer. Host a viewing of this webinar at your library, your faith community, or your support group, and lead a conversation afterward. Bring it to your local paper. Invite your representative's staff. Every conversation about the cold window is one more family that will ask better questions on their hardest day. Thank you for spending this hour with me. The buttons on your screen will take you where you'd like to go next.
